title: Dixit Dominus
hook: Handel at 22, newly arrived in Rome, sets a psalm for five voices and strings, from hammering chords to a hushed duet over a quiet chant.

painting.title: A View of Piazza del Popolo, Rome
painting.collection: Intesa Sanpaolo, Gallerie d'Italia – Palazzo Zevallos Stigliano, Naples
painting.pairingNote: Rome as the young Handel knew it; of the twin churches facing the square, the one on the left, Santa Maria in Montesanto, held the Carmelites’ July feast, one of the occasions at which the Dixit Dominus may first have been sung.

facts: Handel, born in Halle in 1685, had already worked as a violinist, harpsichordist and opera composer in Hamburg when he left for Italy in 1706. In Rome the Pope had banned opera, so music lived in the palaces and churches of wealthy cardinals and princes, and the young Saxon soon had powerful patrons among them.

*Dixit Dominus* sets Psalm 110 (109 in the Latin Bible), “The Lord said unto my Lord”, one of the psalms sung at Vespers, the evening service. Handel probably began it in Venice, on Venetian paper, and dated the finished score in Rome, April 1707. It is the earliest of his manuscripts to survive.

Where and when it was first sung is not known. Scholars have suggested Easter or the first days of May 1707, or the Carmelite feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in mid-July, in 1707 or 1708, at Santa Maria in Montesanto, a church under the protection of Cardinal Carlo Colonna. There is no document to settle it.

It is written for five solo singers (two sopranos, alto, tenor, bass), a five-part choir and strings with two viola parts, over the [[continuo|continuo]]. In Italy Handel met Alessandro Scarlatti and heard the music of Corelli and Vivaldi; the Dixit Dominus is Italian in its brilliance and German in its dense [[counterpoint|counterpoint]], and full of word-painting.
bigPicture.inOneLine: the Lord’s command (I), two solo songs (II–III), an oath and a priesthood (IV–V), judgement and battle (VI–VII), a quiet duet by the brook (VIII), and a blazing doxology that brings back the opening chant (IX).

movements.heading: Dixit Dominus Domino meo
movements.title: Dixit Dominus Domino meo
movements.summary: “The Lord said unto my Lord: sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.” A large, driving movement in G minor for choir, solo voices and strings. Against the busy counterpoint Handel sets a slow church chant, sung in long notes by the sopranos.

mainIdeas.name: “Dixit”
mainIdeas.description: short, punched-out chords on the word “said”, returning again and again.

mainIdeas.name: The chant
mainIdeas.description: a plain psalm tone from [[plainchant|plainchant]], held in long notes as a [[cantus-firmus|cantus firmus]] while the other voices race around it.

stops.hear: The strings set off at speed, with sharp repeated notes
stops.happening: The opening [[ritornello|ritornello]]

stops.hear: The voices burst in with short, hammered chords on “Dixit”
stops.happening: “Dixit Dominus Domino meo” (“The Lord said unto my Lord”)

stops.hear: Single voices step out, soprano, alto and tenor in turn, answered by the full group
stops.happening: “Sede a dextris meis” (“sit thou at my right hand”), solo against [[tutti|tutti]]

stops.hear: The sopranos sing slow, plain notes like church chant, while the other voices and strings rush on around them
stops.happening: “Donec ponam inimicos tuos” (“until I make thine enemies”), with the chant as a cantus firmus

stops.hear: The word “scabellum” (“footstool”) is tossed from voice to voice
stops.happening: “Scabellum pedum tuorum” (“thy footstool”)

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A last, emphatic cadence in G minor
stops.happening: The end

notice: Follow the chant at about two and a half minutes: long, even notes in the top voice, as if a much older piece of music were being carried along inside a new one. It comes back in the last movement.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Scholars Baroque Ensemble, founded in 1987 by the bass David van Asch, sing and play with one voice and one instrument to a part: five singers, who are both the soloists and the choir, two violins, two violas, cello, violone and organ, and no conductor. The result is lean and clear rather than grand. It was recorded in All Saints Church, East Finchley, in London, in October 1994; on the album the Dixit Dominus is tracks 1–9, followed by Handel’s *Salve Regina* and *Nisi Dominus*, both also from 1707.

movements.heading: Virgam virtutis tuae
movements.title: Virgam virtutis tuae
movements.summary: “The Lord shall send the rod of thy power out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.” A short [[aria|aria]] for alto, sung here by a countertenor, with only the continuo beneath it: a forceful, declamatory solo.

mainIdeas.name: The voice
mainIdeas.description: strong, proclaiming phrases, with quick runs on the words of power and rule.

mainIdeas.name: The bass line
mainIdeas.description: cello and organ, walking steadily under the voice.

stops.hear: Cello and organ alone play a firm, striding bass
stops.happening: The continuo introduction

stops.hear: The countertenor enters with bold, proclaiming phrases
stops.happening: “Virgam virtutis tuae emittet Dominus ex Sion” (“The Lord shall send the rod of thy power out of Zion”)

stops.hear: Longer runs of quick notes
stops.happening: “Dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum” (“rule thou in the midst of thine enemies”)

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The bass line closes the aria alone
stops.happening: The end

notice: Only two or three instruments accompany the singer. Notice how much space this leaves around the voice after the crowded first movement.

movements.heading: Tecum principium
movements.title: Tecum principium
movements.summary: “In the day of thy power shall the people offer thee free-will offerings with an holy worship; from the womb before the morning star have I begotten thee.” A graceful soprano aria in an elegant dance rhythm, sung by Kym Amps.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a lilting rhythm in three, close to the Italian corrente, the [[courante|courante]].

mainIdeas.name: The voice
mainIdeas.description: long, smooth phrases that float above the strings.

stops.hear: The strings begin a gentle, lilting dance
stops.happening: The introduction

stops.hear: The soprano enters with a smooth, curving melody
stops.happening: “Tecum principium in die virtutis tuae” (“In the day of thy power”)

stops.hear: The melody moves to new keys and grows more intense
stops.happening: “Ex utero ante luciferum genui te” (“from the womb before the morning star have I begotten thee”)

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The strings round off the dance
stops.happening: The end

notice: After the force of the first two movements, this is music of light. Listen for the moment the voice reaches its highest notes, held and then released.

movements.heading: Juravit Dominus
movements.title: Juravit Dominus
movements.summary: “The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent.” The choir returns: slow, solemn chords for the oath, with sudden, rapid replies for “and will not repent”.

mainIdeas.name: The oath
mainIdeas.description: slow, heavy chords with strange, clashing harmonies.

mainIdeas.name: The reply
mainIdeas.description: quick, repeated notes, like an urgent insistence.

stops.hear: Slow, grave chords from choir and strings, the harmony shifting in unexpected directions
stops.happening: “Juravit Dominus” (“The Lord hath sworn”)

stops.hear: Sudden quick, chattering repeated notes in voices and strings
stops.happening: “Et non poenitebit eum” (“and will not repent”)

stops.hear: The slow oath and the quick reply alternate
stops.happening: The two ideas set against each other

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A final slow cadence
stops.happening: The end

notice: Listen for the contrast of speed: almost frozen chords, then a burst of rapid notes. The music acts out the difference between a solemn vow and the firmness behind it.

movements.heading: Tu es sacerdos
movements.title: Tu es sacerdos
movements.summary: “Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.” A fast, busy chorus in which a short theme enters in one voice after another, a [[fugue|fugue]] at speed.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: quick, patter-like repeated syllables on “Tu es sacerdos in aeternum”.

mainIdeas.name: The second idea
mainIdeas.description: “secundum ordinem Melchisedech”, woven in against it.

stops.hear: A quick, chattering theme in one voice, then another, then another
stops.happening: The fugue on “Tu es sacerdos in aeternum” (“Thou art a priest for ever”)

stops.hear: All five voices are busy at once, the strings doubling them
stops.happening: “Secundum ordinem Melchisedech” (“after the order of Melchizedek”) combined with the first theme

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: The voices come together for a firm close
stops.happening: The end

notice: Try to follow the theme into each new voice: high, then lower, then lower still. With one singer on each part, every entry is easy to hear.

movements.heading: Dominus a dextris tuis
movements.title: Dominus a dextris tuis
movements.summary: “The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath.” The solo voices begin together in a flowing texture; then the choir takes over with sharp, violent chords for the breaking of kings.

mainIdeas.name: The solo group
mainIdeas.description: five voices weaving smooth lines.

mainIdeas.name: “Confregit”
mainIdeas.description: hard, broken-off chords on “he shall strike through”.

stops.hear: The solo voices sing together in smooth, overlapping lines
stops.happening: “Dominus a dextris tuis” (“The Lord at thy right hand”)

stops.hear: The full choir breaks in with short, hammered chords and rushing strings
stops.happening: “Confregit in die irae suae reges” (“shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath”)

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A loud, final cadence
stops.happening: The end

notice: Listen for the change from the soft solo group to the full force of the choir: the music turns from blessing to judgement in a moment.

movements.heading: Judicabit in nationibus
movements.title: Judicabit in nationibus
movements.summary: “He shall judge among the nations; he shall fill the places with dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries.” The most violent movement, a sequence of vivid word-pictures: ruins falling, and heads being shattered, heard as hammered, broken syllables.

mainIdeas.name: “Judicabit”
mainIdeas.description: a vigorous theme passed between the voices.

mainIdeas.name: “Implebit ruinas”
mainIdeas.description: runs that tumble downwards.

mainIdeas.name: “Conquassabit”
mainIdeas.description: the word cut into separate, hammered syllables, “con-quas-sa-bit”, over pounding strings.

stops.hear: A strong theme in the voices and strings, entering one after another
stops.happening: “Judicabit in nationibus” (“He shall judge among the nations”)

stops.hear: Lines that tumble downwards, voice after voice
stops.happening: “Implebit ruinas” (“he shall fill the places with ruins”)

stops.hear: The choir chops the words into short, separate syllables, like blows, while the strings pound
stops.happening: “Conquassabit capita” (“he shall shatter the heads”), word-painting at its most graphic

stops.hear: The texture widens again
stops.happening: “In terra multorum” (“in the land of many”)

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A massive closing cadence
stops.happening: The end

notice: At “conquassabit” the singers stop singing lines and start striking notes. Listen to how the syllables pass between the voices, so that the blows seem to come from every side.

movements.heading: De torrente in via bibet
movements.title: De torrente in via bibet
movements.summary: “He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head.” After the violence, the stillest music in the work: two sopranos in a slow, aching duet, over a soft chant from the tenors and basses and quiet repeated chords in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The duet
mainIdeas.description: two soprano lines that rub against each other, one holding a note while the other moves, then changing places.

mainIdeas.name: The men
mainIdeas.description: a low, almost whispered chant underneath.

stops.hear: Soft, pulsing chords in the strings
stops.happening: The introduction, in C minor

stops.hear: The tenors and basses quietly intone the words
stops.happening: “De torrente in via bibet” (“He shall drink of the brook in the way”)

stops.hear: The two sopranos enter, their lines crossing and clashing gently
stops.happening: The duet: held notes that clash, then resolve

stops.hear: The upper voices rise
stops.happening: “Propterea exaltabit caput” (“therefore shall he lift up the head”)

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The music fades into a soft close
stops.happening: The end

notice: Listen for the small rubs between the two sopranos: one holds a note while the other moves to a clashing one, and then both slip into a sweet chord. The pattern repeats like slow, tired steps.

movements.heading: Gloria Patri
movements.title: Gloria Patri
movements.summary: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.” The words of praise that close every psalm at Vespers, set as a brilliant finale. At “as it was in the beginning” the chant of the first movement returns, and the work ends with a fugue on “Amen”.

mainIdeas.name: “Gloria”
mainIdeas.description: fast, leaping, ringing lines for choir and strings.

mainIdeas.name: The chant
mainIdeas.description: the slow psalm tone from the first movement, back in long notes.

mainIdeas.name: “Amen”
mainIdeas.description: a fugue, entering voice by voice.

stops.hear: The choir and strings break out in fast, leaping phrases
stops.happening: “Gloria Patri” (“Glory be to the Father”)

stops.hear: The music drives on through new keys with rushing runs
stops.happening: “Et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto” (“and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit”)

stops.hear: The sopranos hold the slow chant in long notes, as in the first movement
stops.happening: “Sicut erat in principio” (“as it was in the beginning”), with the cantus firmus

stops.hear: Short themes enter one voice after another, overlapping
stops.happening: “Et in saecula saeculorum. Amen” (“world without end. Amen”), as a fugue

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Everyone joins in the final Amen, ending firmly in G minor
stops.happening: The end

notice: “As it was in the beginning”: Handel takes the words literally and brings back the music of his beginning, the chant of the first movement.

threads.title: The chant
threads.body: An old psalm tone, sung in long notes, appears in the first movement and returns in the last, at the words “as it was in the beginning”.

threads.title: Words made audible
threads.body: Hammered syllables for shattered heads, tumbling runs for ruins, a whispered chant for the brook: Handel paints the psalm line by line, as he would later do in his oratorios.

threads.title: One to a part
threads.body: In this recording every line is sung or played by one performer, so the choir is also the group of soloists, and every strand of the counterpoint can be heard.
